self_review.description: The human-likeness half of write→check→fix. The deterministic checker catches the mechanizable tells; these are the texture checks it cannot verify. The calling model runs each against its OWN draft and rewrites every weak spot before returning. Each item has an id, a one-line `short`, the full `detail`, `applies_to` (['all'] or canonical content types) and an optional `history` for maintainers. The check_text report's manual_review carries the `short` lines for the content_type by default and the `detail` texts when called with rubric="full"; `history` is never served. Edit here and git-push to update; the server makes no API call.

items.short: Check that claims, numbers, names, stance and the requested tone match the source, and that a new draft invents no name, number, date, quote or experience.
items.detail: Confirm that claims, numbers, names and stance are unchanged from the source and that the tone the user asked for is intact (AR-001). In a new draft, confirm every name, number, date, quotation and first-person experience came from the user or the source, with a marked placeholder where one is missing.

items.short: Read the draft in your head and recombine or split any run of sentences that march at one length and shape, starting with runs of short fragments.
items.detail: Read the draft in your head and listen for a run of sentences that march at one cadence, each the same length and shape. Look hardest at runs of short punchline fragments and one-line questions, because that is the cadence problem to find. Recombine or split those sentences by meaning until each carries one whole thought. The checker reports sentence-length numbers, and this item is the qualitative read.

items.short: Count each rhetorical shape (antithesis, copula maxim, rule of three) across the whole piece and vary the construction wherever one repeats.
items.detail: The same construction restated across the piece reads as a tic even when the words differ, whether it is an antithesis ('not X, but Y'), a copula maxim or a rule of three. Vary the constructions as well as the vocabulary. A budget such as 'at most one antithesis', 'at most one appended label' or 'at most one aphorism' covers the whole piece, and checking section by section cannot enforce it, because four sections can each pass with one instance while the document holds four. Count these across every section. The checker counts some of these shapes and reports a document_budget finding, but only within the text it receives, so run the last humanizer_check_text on the assembled document as well as on the part you edited last. The shapes no detector finds are yours to count.
items.history: The four mechanized shapes (BS-011, BS-018, BS-038, BS-039) are counted automatically and reported as a document_budget finding, only within the text handed to the checker. See caveats.per_section_checks_miss_document_budgets.

items.short: Count every 'X, not Y' contrast and every negation flip ('It's not X. It's Y.') across the whole piece, and recast the repeats as positive claims.
items.detail: One contrast is ordinary writing. The tell is the reflex, the same binary reached for in section after section. The checker flags the copula frame ('It is X, not Y.') and leaves the other contrasts to you, such as "We chose depth, not breadth." and "The wordmark comes from paint on paper, not the polished apps she gave up on." A single contracted negation flip ('It's not X. It's Y.', 'This isn't a bug. It's a feature.') is also a judgment call counted across the whole piece, because the checker reports contracted flips as a document_budget finding only when the text holds two or more. The uncontracted form ('It is not a tool. It is a partner.') is flagged on its own, even once. Count every contrast and every flip across the whole piece, and rewrite the repeats as a positive claim that stands on its own.
items.history: BS-011 fires only on a copula plus a clause-final Y. BS-066 counts every negation flip, contracted or not, toward a document budget of one and reports from the second; a single uncontracted flip is still reported as BS-013. See caveats.contrastive_scope_notes_are_the_same_shape.

items.short: Let each section's texture follow its job, and check that the piece does not hold one flat style from start to finish.
items.detail: Check whether the style shifts between sections or holds one flat fingerprint throughout. Human writers modulate, and LLMs stay even. Let each section's texture follow its job, and do not make sections differ for contrast. The checker reports cross-section uniformity, and this item is the qualitative read.

items.short: Cut smooth but empty phrasing, reflexive hedges and motivational closers, and keep the concrete details the source or the user gives.
items.detail: Ask whether this could have been written about almost any topic, by almost anyone. Cut smooth but empty phrasing, reflexive hedges and motivational closers. State the point of view the user or the source holds, and keep the concrete, specific, checkable details the source or the user gives, never invented (see AR-001).

items.short: Find abstract nouns acting as the subject of a human verb ('the work decided', 'the layout carries the weight') and give each sentence a person or concrete subject.
items.detail: An abstract noun ('the gap', 'the work', 'the craft', 'the order') used as the subject of an agentive or experiential verb (mattered, decided, kept, taught, carries, carried, holds, demands) reads fluently while no one in the sentence does anything. Metaphorical 'carry' is the most frequent instance and the hardest to hear ('the layout carries the weight', 'the silence carried the room', 'eight words to carry'), because the verb performs gravity while the sentence names no actor and no effect. Prefer a human or concrete subject, and say what the thing does. The checker catches the fixed collocations, and the open-ended cases are yours to read for. Time and calendar nouns count too, and they are the hardest to hear because they read as a lively figure ('the Fridays survived', 'Busy season eats the Fridays', 'Billiards survives final year', 'Work does not get to claim them'). Read for a schedule, a job or an activity that 'decides', 'wins' or 'gives back'. Name the person and say what happens ('I still make it to billiards on Fridays'). Ideas and artifacts slip in the same way, most often inside a maxim about the work ('the answer usually costs you the design you arrived with', 'A design that ignores the build comes back', 'the only thing I do that asks me to stand still'). None of these has a word the checker could anchor on.
items.history: The fixed collocations are auto-detected as BS-031; the open-ended abstract-subject cases are this rubric item (server cannot verify reliably; see AP-033, AP-044). The weekday, semester and season frames are mechanized as BS-052 at low confidence. A reviewer flagged all three idea and artifact maxims on a portfolio site in 2026; none has a lexical anchor the checker could use.

items.short: Delete any closer, label or headline that performs insight or closure without adding a fact, and end each section on its last substantive point.
items.detail: A performative framing beat is a sentence or label whose job is to perform insight, closure or self-awareness instead of carrying content. It takes three forms. (a) A self-satisfied closer is a neat aphorism ending a section that adds no new fact, name or number, often crediting the author or pivoting on a tidy antithesis ('The data set is public; the reading of it is mine.'). (b) First-person meta-commentary on the work itself ('my take', 'the reading of it is mine', 'as I see it') turns up in a piece meant to be evidence-led. (c) A clever paradox headline is used to sound sharp where a plain statement of the point would do. Delete the beat and end on the last substantive point. Keep at most one aphoristic or paradox construction per piece, and only where it does analytical work. The device is human in moderation, and the tell is repetition and substitution for content. A standalone meta-label ('in 200 words', 'in brief') is the same beat. Short cells and captions have their own versions, such as the clipped verdict that performs a decision ('Tutoring stays.'), the stance closer that points back at a number already given ('and I want to keep it there') and the tidy aphoristic closer that rounds off a plain list ('four months is a long time to wait', 'tires me out more than any lecture did'). Replace each with the next concrete fact. Captions have a numeric version, the verbless pair that sets one against many ('One count, four moments', 'Three sizes, all the same height.', 'One app, every chat.'). Ordinary terse writing uses the same shape ('Two adults, one child.', 'Two tablets, every four hours.', 'Three goals, one assist.'), so judge each pair by whether it reports a fact or performs one. A maxim that hands the verdict to a third party is the same beat ('and the developer is right to send it back').
items.history: The standalone meta-label form is auto-detected as BS-022; the closer overlaps BS-018; see AP-035, AP-033. The clipped verdict is BS-053 and the stance closer BS-054. The numeric caption pair could not be mechanized, because ordinary terse writing has the same shape (see AP-069).

items.short: Keep the caveats, exceptions and open points the source has instead of smoothing every thread into a neat resolution, and add none it lacks.
items.detail: Check whether every point lines up too neatly, with each example fitting perfectly, every thread resolved and no loose ends or tension left. Human writing has friction, such as a caveat that complicates the thesis, a digression, an example that only mostly fits or a point left partly open. A frictionless argument is itself a tell. Keep the friction the source has (a caveat, an exception, a point left open) instead of smoothing it away, and add none it lacks (AR-001).

items.short: Read every heading and dek, cut any part after the comma that only says the subject matters, and allow one such label per document at most.
items.detail: An appended significance label is a heading, subtitle or dek that names its subject and then annexes a second element promising the subject matters. It can be a reduced relative ('Reintegration support at the moment of release, and the officer the whole system turns on.'), an appositive that asserts a hinge, or a WH clause pre-defending a choice ('Method, and why this one'). Read every label in the piece and ask whether the part after the comma adds a fact or only tells the reader this is important. Cut it and let the section earn it. One such label may be deliberate. Two or more in one piece is the tell, because a repeated rhetorical shape is what reads as machine-made. The budget is one per document, counted across the assembled whole, because each check sees only the text it is given. The checker catches the WH form, and the reduced-relative and appositive forms are yours to read for, as in 'The rebuild, and the one decision that made it possible.' and 'Nine months of rework, and the meeting that started it.'
items.history: The WH form is mechanized as BS-038. The reduced-relative and appositive forms need a parser the server does not have (see AP-051), and three attempts to mechanize the appositive form are recorded in caveats.labels_are_where_the_tells_hide. check_text is stateless (see caveats.per_section_checks_miss_document_budgets).

items.short: Before the final rubric="full" check, read for stale figures, words that can go and passives that hide who acted, then confirm prohibitions_clear on the result.
items.detail: Run this pass (the Orwell pass) after the fix rounds and before the final rubric="full" check on the assembled document, and read the draft once more for three marks of flabby prose that the other layers miss. (a) Look for stale figures of speech, meaning any image you did not choose deliberately ('moves the needle', 'the federal purse', 'the tip of the iceberg'). The checker knows a closed list, and the class is open, so read for it. Replace the figure with the number or the name it stood in for and leave out any fresher figure. (b) Cut every word that can go. This rule does the most work in anything longer than a page, and the padding phrases in lexical_patterns.orwell.padding_phrases are a starting point for it. (c) Use the active where it will do and name who did it, keeping the passive in method and regulatory writing where it is the norm. One carve-out always applies. A domain term with no everyday equivalent (statutory release, Protected B, an API, a subpoena) is defined in plain words at first use and then used plainly. Do not swap it for a vaguer everyday word, because that loses the meaning the argument runs on. Then run humanizer_check_text on the trimmed text and confirm prohibitions_clear is true, because cutting words can create or expose findings such as a comma splice or a new run-on.
items.history: A closed list of stale figures is auto-detected as BS-041. The passive is deliberately not mechanized, because the legitimate passive is common in method and regulatory writing. See lexical_patterns.orwell and caveats.jargon_substitution_loses_meaning.

items.short: Change constructions and section texture as well as words, because vocabulary swaps alone leave the draft's shape as it was.
items.detail: Section-to-section variation is among the most durable human signals, and word swaps alone leave the draft's shape as it was. Look past vocabulary to the constructions and to how each section reads, and keep the plain word where it is the right one.

items.short: Read every run of three or more sentences that open the same way, keep one only if it builds, and cut the repetition where each limb restates the first.
items.detail: Anaphora means three or more consecutive sentences opening on the same word or the same two words ('They assume users will pay. They assume the market is ready. They assume nothing changes.'). Read the run and decide whether the repetition does work or fills space. The form itself is legitimate and has a name. Thoreau wrote 'It does not keep the country free. It does not settle the West. It does not educate.', and Melville 'Forty years of continual whaling! Forty years of privation, and peril, and storm-time!' (deliberate anaphora that builds). The tell is the same construction used without escalation, where each limb restates the first instead of advancing it, and where cutting the repetition would cost the passage nothing. The figure and the tell share one syntax, so the checker cannot separate them and this one is yours to judge. The checker catches only a run that opens on This, These or the pronoun it. Allow at most one deliberate anaphoric run per document, counted across the assembled whole, and make it the strongest passage in the piece. If it is not, cut it.
items.history: Every formulation tried scored 0/15 precision on human prose (see caveats.rhetorical_figures_defeat_shape_detection). Only the This/These/It chain is auto-detected, as BS-009. The document budget follows caveats.per_section_checks_miss_document_budgets.

items.short: Cut any sentence that explains what the image, line or example before it already showed.
items.detail: Check whether a sentence explains what the image, line or example before it already showed ('He slammed the door. He was angry.'). Professional writers often cut this kind of sentence from LLM drafts, and newer models still write it. Cut the explanation and trust the reader.
items.history: Professional writers cut this in about a fifth of their edits to LLM drafts, and it does not go away as models improve (Chakrabarty, Laban and Wu, CHI 2025).

items.short: In an essay, post, opinion piece or cover letter, look for one I, you or question to the reader, and add one only where it states a position the source holds.
items.detail: This applies to essays, blog posts, opinion pieces and cover letters, and leaves reference and technical copy alone. Check whether the piece holds a single I, you or question to the reader. LLM essays use markedly less interactional language (stance, engagement and questions to the reader) than human ones. Add one only where it carries a position the user or the source holds, and never as decoration.
items.history: Jiang and Hyland, English for Specific Purposes, 2025.

items.short: Use 'says' for every quote attribution, and drop bold-label bullets, emoji at the start of lines and stock names unless the house style wants them.
items.detail: Readers recognise a set of defaults. Quote attributions rotate through 'notes', 'explains' and 'emphasizes' where a reporter would write 'says' every time. Every bullet opens with a bold label and a colon. Emoji sit at the start of headings or bullets. Characters get stock names ('Emily', 'Sarah', 'Dr. Chen', 'Elara'). Expert annotators cite each of these. Use the plain form unless the house style asks for the other one.

items.short: Cut a ', so' tail that only tells the reader the first half was good, and keep it where the reader needs the causal link.
items.detail: A cause-to-benefit 'so' tail is a sentence that states a mechanism and then appends ', so' plus the payoff it promises the reader ('Quip updates itself, so a fix reached people within a day of shipping.', 'Only the width changes, so the window stays under the menu-bar icon and nothing jumps away from the pointer.'). It reads as a product brochure explaining its own value. The shape is too common in plain prose for the checker, so read for it. Keep the 'so' when the reader needs the causal link, and cut it when the second half only tells them the first half was good. Often the fix is to keep one half, either the fact or the user's experience of it.
items.history: A reviewer flagged both examples as AI-coded in a 2026 portfolio review; the shape is too common in plain prose to detect.

items.short: State the writer's history as facts with dates or numbers, and cut lines that tell it as a tidy sequence or praise the writer's own habits.
items.detail: Watch for lines that tell the writer's history as a tidy sequence or describe their own habits approvingly, such as 'Ten years of teaching neurodivergent and multilingual learners came first, and so did the habit of watching where people get stuck.', 'Before them came two web tools for English learners.', 'The job was watching someone try to make sense of something complicated...', 'I design the screens, build them in code, and keep the Figma files behind them tidy.' and 'People I've never met use it'. Each sounds like a voice performing modesty or craft. State the fact with its date or number ('Teaching neurodivergent and multilingual learners since 2016.') and drop the adjective about yourself. The shape 'X came first, and so did the habit of Y' is yours to read for, because 'Prices rose, and so did the practice of haggling.' is the same construction in ordinary prose.
items.history: Every attested line was flagged as AI-coded in a 2026 portfolio and résumé review. 'X came first, and so did the habit of Y' could not be mechanized, because 'Prices rose, and so did the practice of haggling.' is the same construction.

items.short: Check that someone who has never used the product could follow each sentence on first read, and rewrite mechanism chains, internal jargon and clever slogans.
items.detail: Ask whether someone who has never used the product could follow each sentence of product, portfolio or case-study copy on first read. Three failures recur. (a) Mechanism is written as a chain of clauses instead of saying what the user gets ('Show them in every space and they stay at the top of the sidebar, with one sign-in and one unread count, while the rest of the list changes.'). (b) The copy uses the product's own internal words, or verbs users never say ('cut across all of them', 'Filing a GIF' (nobody files GIFs), 'nothing of the app is drawn inside Chorus'). (c) A slogan has a second half that is clever and impossible to picture ('Every chat and inbox in one Mac window, and only what's new turns red.'). Also cut vague casual counts ('a dozen or so testers'), run-in labels ('The worst bug:') and release-by-release history ('first release 13 July'). Write short sentences in plain words, use a UX term where it is the right term, and define any product concept before using it.
items.history: All three failures were flagged in a 2026 portfolio review after passing the checker.
